newsitem.title: USA: U.S. refiners show weak appetite for foreign crude.
newsitem.headline: U.S. refiners show weak appetite for foreign crude.

text.p: U.S. refiners showed little appetite for foreign crudes Monday despite a plethora of offers, traders said.
The wide spread between West Texas Intermediate and North Sea Brent has made trans-Atlantic trade economic after a long winter hiatus, traders said.
At least two Wall Street players are trying to sell Brent cargoes into the Gulf Coast. Offers for January Brent are coming in around February WTI minus 20 cents a barrel, traders said.
The influx of foreign barrels has put pressure on domestic sweet grades. Light Louisiana Sweet on Monday traded around WTI/Cushing minus 30 cents a barrel, down 15-30 cents from late Friday.
The spread, rather than refiner demand, seemed to be drawing foreign barrels into the Gulf Coast, one refiner said, noting weak domestic margins.
"Plenty is being offered, but not much is happening," the refiner said. "It's the extremely wide spread, not demand, that's pulling Brent over."
The spread between February WTI and Brent stood around $1.50-55 a barrel.
Meanwhile, Iraq's State Oil Marketing Organization (SOMO) has so far signed 21 supply contracts under the U.N. brokered oil-for-food deal. The U.N. had approved 16 contracts by December 20.

In Latin America, an fob cargo of Colombian sweet Cusiana crude for January 23-24 is on offer at around March WTI plus 40 cents, although the going price is likely to be around 30-35 cents premium, traders said.
In the U.S. aftermarket, a series of partial paper February Brent cargoes changed hands at $23.25 a barrel, up five cents from the London close.
Intermonth spreads were softer, with Jan/Feb Brent trading at 36 cents, down from 45 cents over the day.
Feb/Mar Brent was done at 50 cents, down 11 cents from the IPE settlement.
